items.title: Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics centres on agape
items.claim: What is the central principle of Fletcher's situation ethics?

options.text: There are no moral rules of any kind
The single absolute is agape (selfless love); all other rules are guidelines that can be overridden when love requires it. Set out in 'Situation Ethics: The New Morality' (1966)
Maximise pleasure for the greatest number

items.reveal:
Fletcher's six propositions: (1) Only love is intrinsically good. (2) The ruling norm of Christian decision is love, not law. (3) Love and justice are the same — justice is love distributed. (4) Love wills the neighbour's good. (5) Only the end justifies the means. (6) Love's decisions are made situationally, not prescriptively.

Fletcher gave four working principles: pragmatism, relativism, positivism, personalism.

The Vatican condemned situation ethics under Pius XII (1956, before Fletcher's book) and again in the 1990s. Critics argue that 'love' as the only criterion is too vague to guide decisions; defenders argue agape has specific content (the New Testament's understanding) that excludes self-interested 'love'.
items.why: Christian ethics in the mid-20th century split between absolutist and contextual approaches. Fletcher's situation ethics is a high-profile example of context-driven ethics — challenging the natural law tradition from within Christianity.

items.title: Judaism centres on covenant — a binding agreement with God
items.claim: What is the relationship between the Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants in Judaism?

options.text: The Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17, sealed by circumcision) promises land and descendants; the Mosaic covenant (Exodus 19-24, at Sinai) gives the Torah law — both remain binding on Jews
There is only one covenant — at Sinai
Covenants applied only to ancient Israelites, not modern Jews

items.reveal:
Brit milah (covenant of circumcision) is performed on Jewish boys on the eighth day after birth, marking the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:11-13). The Mosaic covenant at Sinai (around 1300 BCE in traditional dating) establishes the 613 mitzvot (commandments) of the Torah law.

The Noahide covenant (Genesis 9) — applying to all humanity — is also recognised. Rabbinic Judaism distinguishes seven Noahide laws binding on all people from the 613 mitzvot binding specifically on Jews.

Christianity reinterprets these covenants through 'new covenant' theology (Hebrews 8); Judaism rejects supersessionism — the older covenants are not abrogated.
items.why: Covenant is not a vague concept of relationship. In Judaism it is a specific structure with terms, obligations and consequences — and a major point of theological disagreement with Christianity.

items.title: Shabbat begins on Friday evening, not Saturday
items.claim: When does the Jewish Sabbath begin and end?

options.text: It runs from Saturday morning to Sunday morning
From sunset on Friday to the appearance of three stars on Saturday night — Jewish days begin at sunset, following Genesis 1's 'and there was evening and there was morning'
It is calculated by the Gregorian clock

items.reveal:
The Genesis creation account marks each day 'there was evening and there was morning' — establishing the Jewish day as evening to evening. Shabbat is welcomed with candle lighting (typically 18 minutes before sunset) and Kiddush over wine.

The Torah commands rest from melacha — 39 categories of work derived from the activities involved in building the Tabernacle. These include lighting fires, writing, carrying in public, tearing, cooking. Modern applications (electricity, driving, mobile phones) follow rabbinic reasoning by analogy.

Shabbat ends with Havdalah — a brief ceremony with wine, spices and a multi-wick candle separating the holy from the ordinary.
items.why: Religious time is structured differently. Treating Shabbat as 'Saturday' misses both its beginning at sunset and the depth of its observance — which is one of the most distinctive elements of Jewish practice.
